Article.ArticleTitle: The infrapatellar fat pad-synovium immunometabolic interface in knee osteoarthritis: a local amplifier of joint inflammation.

Abstract.AbstractText: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a whole-joint disease in which synovitis is associated with pain and structural progression. The infrapatellar fat pad (IPFP) lies next to the anterior synovium and contains adipocytes, mesenchymal and fibroblast-like stromal cells, macrophages, vascular cells, and nerves. Alongside its mechanical cushioning role, the IPFP releases adipokines, cytokines, chemokines, lipid mediators, and extracellular vesicles. Adipocyte stress, matrix remodeling, fibrosis, and immune cell accumulation alter this secretory profile in OA. Single-cell analyses of paired human tissues suggest that the IPFP and synovium may share mesenchymal progenitors and undergo coordinated inflammatory and profibrotic remodeling. We propose that these tissues form an immunometabolic interface in which macrophages integrate lipid and damage signals, while stromal cells recruit immune cells and remodel the extracellular matrix (ECM). These interactions may link local metabolic dysfunction to persistent synovitis, cartilage catabolism, and pain. Human evidence, however, comes largely from cross-sectional studies of tissues collected during surgery for advanced OA. Computational predictions of cell-cell communication require functional testing, and animal interventions cannot establish causality in humans. The interface is therefore best regarded as a potential local amplifier of inflammation; its role in disease initiation remains unproven. Longitudinal studies with spatial resolution and interventions stratified by phenotype are needed to determine when, in which patients, and through which components the interface has therapeutic value.

Article.ArticleTitle: Network Biology: Current Status, Applications, Challenges, and Future Prospects.

Abstract.AbstractText: Network biology provides a systems-level framework for understanding how interactions among molecular components, cells, microbial communities, tissues, and organs generate biological function and disease phenotypes. Recent advances in multiomics, single-cell and spatial profiling, network inference, organoid and organ-on-chip technologies, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence have shifted the field from static molecular maps toward dynamic, multiscale, and predictive network models. Major branches include molecular interaction networks, intracellular regulatory networks, single-cell and multicellular networks, microbial networks, disease networks, and interorgan interaction networks. Experimental and computational approaches are compared with respect to network reconstruction, causal validation, and cross-scale integration. Biomedical applications span disease classification, biomarker discovery, therapeutic-target identification, drug-response prediction, regenerative medicine, and precision healthcare. Particular emphasis is placed on interorgan interaction networks, in which carrier, route, range, timescale, recipient specificity, directionality, and feedback are treated as distinct mechanistic dimensions while mechanistic confidence is distinguished from translational maturity. Persistent challenges include incomplete context-specific network reconstruction, uncertain causal directionality, limited cross-scale integration, model interpretability, and insufficient clinical validation. Further progress will depend on integrating longitudinal and perturbation-resolved measurements with human-relevant experimental systems and multiscale computational models that quantify uncertainty and support prospective validation of patient-specific predictions.

Article.ArticleTitle: Mapping DEHP-induced metabolic dysregulation through multi-omics and systems biology: an adverse outcome pathway network approach.

Abstract.AbstractText: Di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) is a widespread endocrine-disrupting plasticizer associated with metabolic disorders. To elucidate their mechanistic basis, we developed an Adverse Outcome Pathway Network (AOPN) informed by DEHP-induced perturbations, by integrating multi-omics data, systems biology modeling, and targeted literature evidence. Multi-omics data were generated in 3D human hepatic cells, pancreatic β-cells, and zebrafish larvae exposed to DEHP across biologically relevant concentration ranges. Transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses revealed perturbations in lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function and oxidative stress pathways, including altered sphingolipid signaling and dysregulation of sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P). Systems biology modeling contextualized these perturbations within metabolic pathways and generated dose-dependent predictions for key intermediates, highlighting potential reinforcing feedback mechanisms such as ATP-ROS interactions that may further destabilize metabolic homeostasis. Integrating experimental and literature evidence identified key event relationships proposed to link early molecular perturbations to downstream adverse metabolic outcomes, including hepatic steatosis, insulin resistance, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), and obesity. Central mechanistic features of the network converge on lipid remodeling, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, serine/S1P pathway disruption, and impaired insulin signaling. Because the individual omics contrasts are based on three replicates per condition, statistical support in this work is evaluated at pathway rather than single-feature level: under Benjamini-Hochberg control almost no individual transcript is significant, whereas the pathways carrying the mitochondrial and lipid-handling key events remain significant in competitive gene-set tests. Cross-system comparison showed that suppression of oxidative-energy metabolism is the only module conserved across all three systems, whereas PPAR signalling and fatty-acid handling are liver-specific and non-monotonic. Together, these data support a coherent, evidence-integrating mechanistic hypothesis linking early molecular events to adverse metabolic outcomes across multiple levels of biological organization, rather than a quantitatively validated causal pathway. To our knowledge, this study provides a novel integrative AOPN framework combining multi-omics data across liver and pancreatic models and reveals previously underappreciated metabolic cross-talk, including involvement of serine and S1P pathways. The proposed framework is explicitly hypothesis-generating and evidence-integrating: it provides a transparent, FDR-audited basis for future quantitative AOP development and supports mechanistically informed chemical risk assessment by identifying early key events, potential biomarkers, and intervention points relevant to human metabolic health.

Article.ArticleTitle: Single-Cell Resolution Mapping of Osteoarthritis-Associated Chondrocyte Dynamics Using a High-Density CMOS MEA Platform.

Abstract.AbstractText: Fibrosis is a major cause of chronic tissue dysfunction and contributes substantially to morbidity and mortality worldwide. Osteoarthritis (OA), affecting over 590 million people, is a prevalent fibrotic joint disease for which disease-modifying therapies remain lacking, partly because disease progression remains incompletely understood. As human-relevant in vitro models, including organ-on-chip and microphysiological systems, become increasingly important, non-invasive technologies capable of continuous cellular monitoring are urgently needed. Here, we implement high-density complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) multielectrode array (MEA)-based impedance profiling as a label-free platform for longitudinal assessment of OA-relevant chondrocyte remodeling. Human primary chondrocytes cultured on CMOS-MEA chips exhibited impedance increases that correlated with electrode occupancy and extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition. Spatial impedance mapping enabled visualization of injury-response dynamics, while oxidative stress induced progressive impedance decline accompanied by apoptosis, morphological remodeling, and chondrocyte dedifferentiation, evidenced by reduced collagen II and SOX9 expression and increased collagen I expression. In contrast, osteogenic de-differentiation produced increased impedance associated with ECM remodeling and matrix mineralization. Together, these findings support high-density CMOS-MEA impedance profiling as a non-invasive approach for monitoring cellular remodeling and provide a foundation for future integration of spatially resolved impedance sensing into advanced microphysiological systems for OA and other fibrotic diseases.

Article.ArticleTitle: A Combined Network Toxicology and Docking Study to Identify Putative Molecular Targets Linking Styrene Exposure to Atherosclerosis.

Abstract.AbstractText: Styrene is a ubiquitous volatile organic compound linked to hematologic and vascular alterations; however, the molecular mechanisms connecting exposure to atherosclerosis remain poorly characterized.

We integrated peripheral blood mononuclear cell transcriptomic profiles (GSE23746) with toxicogenomic data from the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database, applying support vector machine recursive feature elimination and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator machine learning algorithms to identify core targets at the styrene-atherosclerosis intersection. Immune infiltration was assessed using CIBERSORT and single-sample gene set enrichment analysis, and molecular docking evaluated binding potential.

Four model genes-CCND3, CCR1, MYC, and MYD88-were identified and constituted a diagnostic signature with high accuracy (area under the curve > 0.9). These genes were enriched in IL-17 and NF-κB inflammatory pathways and correlated with distinct immune cell alterations, particularly neutrophils and T cell subsets. Molecular docking predicted direct, moderate-affinity binding of styrene to CCND3 (Vina score = -6.4 kcal/mol), involving multiple contacts within the cyclin domain.

The convergence of transcriptomic screening and molecular docking identifies CCND3 as a putative target for styrene-protein interaction and suggests a mechanistic hypothesis linking styrene to atherosclerosis via inflammatory and immune dysregulation. The computational framework provides a basis for future experimental validation.

This computational framework generates the hypothesis that styrene may contribute to atherosclerosis through coordinated perturbations of immune signaling and cell cycle regulation, with CCND3 representing a candidate molecular target for future experimental validation in styrene-exposed populations.

Article.ArticleTitle: Single-cell Transcriptomics in Autoimmune Diseases: Mechanistic Insights, Cross-disease Convergence, and Translational Challenges in Rheumatoid Arthritis, Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, Type 1 Diabetes, and Multiple Sclerosis.

Abstract.AbstractText: Autoimmune diseases are characterized by loss of immune tolerance and substantial heterogeneity across patients, tissues, and disease stages. Although bulk transcriptomic studies have identified important inflammatory pathways, they cannot directly resolve rare, transitional, and tissue-contextualized cell states that may be relevant to disease mechanisms and therapeutic response. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables transcriptomic profiling at cellular resolution, while complementary multimodal, receptor-repertoire, epigenomic, and spatial approaches can link cellular states to protein phenotype, clonal architecture, regulatory programs, and tissue context. This review critically examines recent single-cell studies in rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus and lupus nephritis, type 1 diabetes, and multiple sclerosis. Rather than providing a descriptive catalogue of published studies, we assess the strength of available evidence by distinguishing independently replicated findings from observations supported by limited studies, and cross-sectional associations from longitudinal, treatment-response, and functional evidence. Across the selected diseases, studies repeatedly report inflammatory programs involving interferon signaling, chemokine-mediated immune recruitment, and stromal-immune interactions; however, evidence for convergence at the cell-state and regulatory-network levels remains limited, and the extent to which shared signatures represent common pathogenic mechanisms rather than inflammatory context remains uncertain. We evaluate the translational potential of scRNA-seq for biomarker discovery, patient stratification, and treatment response prediction, while considering evidence from related tissue-based molecular stratification approaches, including the R4RA randomized trial in rheumatoid arthritis. R4RA provides prospective randomized evidence that synovial molecular features can enrich for differential therapeutic responses, but its use of bulk synovial transcriptomics and histopathology does not constitute prospective validation of single-cell-derived biomarkers. We further highlight cohort biases, reproducibility challenges, dissociation artifacts, computational ambiguity, and privacy concerns that constrain immediate clinical implementation. Together, these advances position single-cell profiling as a mechanistic discovery platform with substantial translational promise, contingent on standardization, validation across diverse cohorts, and integration with functional perturbation approaches.

Article.ArticleTitle: Sexual dimorphism in epidermal stem cell dynamics.

Abstract.AbstractText: The epidermis is a stratified epithelium comprising proliferative basal cells and differentiated suprabasal cells that are continuously renewed throughout life. Conflicting theories have been proposed regarding the heterogeneity of the basal cell layer, with some studies proposing that all proliferative cells have self-renewal potential during homeostasis1-5. Meanwhile, others posit a model in which stem cell differentiation occurs through an intermediate transit-amplifying-like progenitor state with strictly limited proliferative potential6-10. Here, to determine the heterogeneity and pattern of cell fate, we performed intravital time-lapse imaging to track the fate of lineage-labelled cells in the skin interfollicular epidermis. Results from quantitative analyses of clonal dynamics support a two-compartment model of epidermal homeostasis, whereby basal cells are organized in a stem cell-transit-amplifying cell hierarchy. Critical to these conclusions was the discovery of sexual dimorphism in epidermal fate, with female mice showing a highly synchronized pattern of cell division, differentiation and delamination that contributes to accelerated wound healing. Single-cell RNA sequencing, transcriptional profiling and clonal analyses of castrated mice revealed that male sex hormones promote stem cell differentiation and delamination. In summary, our study provides insight into the functional identity of the stem cell population and identifies sex-specific differences in the regulation of epidermal stem cells and transit-amplifying cell fate.

Article.ArticleTitle: Transcriptomic reprogramming screen identifies SRSF1 as a regulator of aging.

Abstract.AbstractText: Aging is characterized by progressive functional decline accompanied by distinct transcriptomic and epigenetic alterations. Although partial reprogramming via Yamanaka factors can reverse these signatures and improve cell function, toxicity and efficacy concerns limit their in vivo application, necessitating alternative geroprotective interventions. Here we develop an interpretable transcriptomic age predictor in human fibroblasts and perform a cDNA overexpression screen to identify factors that reprogram aged transcriptomes toward youthful states. This screen identifies the RNA-processing and splicing factor SRSF1 as a regulator of cellular aging that produces robust youthful transcriptional signatures without loss of cellular identity. In vitro, SRSF1 induction restores youthful phenotypes by reducing senescence, proteostatic stress and inflammatory signaling. In aged mice, inducible SRSF1 expression reduces frailty progression by 44% and is associated with a 14% extension of median lifespan (n = 9-10 per group). Our findings establish SRSF1 as a conserved regulator of aging and a promising geroprotective target.

Article.ArticleTitle: RAS pathway mutations orchestrate chromatin reconfiguration and transcriptional rewiring in colorectal cancer.

Abstract.AbstractText: RAS pathway mutations occur in ~ 40% of colorectal cancers (CRCs), with KRAS- and BRAF- mutant tumors exhibiting distinct mutational, transcriptional, and epigenetic landscapes. Advances in next-generation sequencing enable integrated analyses of multi-omics data, providing insight into their regulatory relationships. To define the molecular programs driven by RAS pathway mutations, we generated isogenic CRC cell models and profiled chromatin accessibility using ATAC-seq.

We performed ATAC-seq in isogenic HCT116 and RKO models. Mutation-associated changes in genes, regulatory elements, and signaling pathways were identified, together with inferred transcription factor (TF) binding activity. Clinical datasets were analyzed to assess whether features identified in the cell models were recapitulated in patient tumors and whether they were associated with clinical outcomes.

Isogenic CRC models segregated by RAS pathway mutation status at both epigenetic and transcriptomic levels. Mutation alterations modulated WNT signaling, accompanied by changes in RUNX2 and TCF7L2 expression and binding activity. Comparison between the HCT116 and RKO models identified 85 genes, eight of which displayed reproducible expression patterns across three independent clinical cohorts. TCF7L2 were associated with RAS pathway mutations in patient tumors, with elevated expression level predicting worse overall survival independent of cofactors.

We identified RAS pathway mutation-driven regulatory reprogramming with convergent effects on WNT signaling. TCF7L2 emerged as a key TF, with elevated expression in BRAF-mutant tumors independently associated with poor clinical outcomes. These findings highlight a clinically relevant epigenetic mechanism linking RAS pathway mutations to CRC cell survival maintenance.

Article.ArticleTitle: Multi-omics integration and machine learning identify an ACKR1+ endothelial cell-based lactate-immune signature associated with carotid plaque vulnerability and progression.

Abstract.AbstractText: Early identification of vulnerable carotid plaques is crucial for stroke prevention, but the upstream metabolic processes linked to endothelial transition and immune recruitment remain poorly defined. We characterised lactate metabolism in ACKR1+ endothelial cells (ECs) in human carotid plaques and derived a machine-learning signature for discriminating plaque vulnerability.

Internal and external (GSE253903) single-cell datasets were integrated to identify endothelial subpopulations, and bulk transcriptomic (GSE163154) and in-house proteomic data were used to assess metabolism-immune correlations. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression selected core features for a logistic model, which was locked and applied to three independent cohorts: GSE43292 (Stary stage ≥ IV vs. I-II), GSE28829 (early vs. advanced lesions) and GSE100927 (normal vs. atherosclerotic arteries). Key molecules were validated in situ by immunohistochemistry (IHC) and spatial transcriptomics in independent plaques (five stable, five unstable).

An ACKR1+ EC subpopulation linked to neovascularisation showed hyperactive glycolysis and enhanced lactate metabolism. Computational inference linked lactate accumulation to HIF-1α stability, CXCL12 release and CD8+ T-cell infiltration via the CXCL12-CXCR4 axis, and the monocarboxylate transporters SLC16A3 and SLC16A4 emerged as quantitative readouts of this 'lactate-immune' state. In unstable plaques, IHC confirmed higher atypical chemokine receptor 1 (ACKR1; geometric mean ratio [GMR] = 6.82), CD8+ T-cell density (GMR = 4.63), SLC16A3 (GMR = 4.74) and HIF-1α (GMR = 4.02; all q < .05), with lactylation elevated in the lipid core. A four-feature model (ACKR1, SLC16A3, SLC16A4, CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity score) performed well in training and retained discrimination in the progression-stratified cohorts, while in GSE100927 it showed high disease-identification performance across three arterial beds.

Lactate metabolic reprogramming under hypoxia is associated with ACKR1+ EC-related CD8+ T-cell recruitment and plaque instability. This chain is an association-based hypothesis requiring functional confirmation. The signature discriminates robustly at both the vulnerability-stratification and disease-identification levels, providing a quantifiable framework for molecular classification of atherosclerotic plaques.

Article.ArticleTitle: A lipid-related transcriptomic signature for distinguishing Kawasaki disease from febrile infections: a Mendelian randomization and machine-learning study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Kawasaki disease (KD) diagnosis remains challenging because no pathognomonic test exists and the clinical presentation overlaps extensively with common childhood infections. Acute KD is accompanied by reproducible lipid perturbations, yet whether these changes are causally linked to the innate immune-driven vascular damage of KD vasculitis is unestablished. We aimed to derive a lipid-related transcriptomic signature for distinguishing KD from febrile infections and to characterize its relationship with innate immune remodeling.

Bidirectional two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) screened 422 candidate exposures (419 lipid/metabolic traits and three immune-cell phenotypes) against two independent KD GWAS cohorts, with multiplicity correction. Differentially expressed genes from a training cohort comparing KD with rigorously classified febrile controls were intersected with a broad lipid-metabolism-related GeneCards set, yielding 459 candidates. The 459 candidates were evaluated across 130 machine-learning combinations; a full-training LASSO fit at lambda.1se yielded a 12-gene candidate panel, and the saved penalized model was applied unchanged to an independent cohort without batch correction. The immune microenvironment was estimated using CIBERSORT, acute-to-convalescent expression changes were tracked longitudinally, and selected markers were assessed in TNF-α-stimulated HUVECs.

No exposure survived correction for the 422 tests performed (minimum Benjamini-Hochberg q = 0.979). All nine discovery-stage nominal hits were evaluated in a second KD GWAS; eight had directionally concordant point estimates, but none reached an unadjusted P < 0.05 in the second cohort. The frozen penalized model achieved an external AUC of 0.851 (95% CI 0.768-0.934) in GSE68004 without cross-cohort batch correction. CIBERSORT indicated a higher estimated neutrophil fraction in KD, concordant with a mature-neutrophil marker score from the same matrix. CETP, KREMEN1, and CCL23 were lower in convalescent samples after IVIG (all FDR < 0.0001) and were induced in TNF-α-treated HUVECs, together with VCAM-1, ICAM-1, and IL-8.

The frozen penalized model showed moderate discrimination between KD and febrile controls, but the selected 12-gene set represents one candidate realization of a partition-sensitive modeling pipeline. KREMEN1 warrants separate biological study on the basis of marginal, longitudinal, and immune-association findings rather than its selection stability. Recalibration and prospective validation are required before clinical use. The HUVEC findings are transcriptional and hypothesis-generating.

Article.ArticleTitle: Inflammation-fibrosis crosstalk in endometriosis: immune-stromal mechanisms linking lesion persistence to pain and infertility.

Abstract.AbstractText: Endometriosis is an estrogen-dependent chronic inflammatory disorder in which ectopic endometrial-like tissue undergoes repeated injury, incomplete resolution, and progressive remodeling. Fibrosis is therefore not merely a terminal scar but an active component of lesion biology. Cyclic bleeding activates platelets and innate immune cells, generates iron-dependent oxidative stress and hypoxia, and sustains transforming growth factor-β, sphingosine-1-phosphate, Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/AKT-ERK, and Notch-related signals. These cues promote fibroblast activation, myofibroblast differentiation, extracellular-matrix deposition, and epithelial-, endothelial-, mesothelial-, or macrophage-to-mesenchymal plasticity. The resulting stiff matrix can further reinforce inflammatory, vascular, and neural programs, creating a self-maintaining inflammation-fibrosis circuit. Clinically, this circuit may stabilize ectopic lesions, promote adhesions, increase tissue tension and neurogenic inflammation, damage the ovarian cortex, and perturb the peritoneal and eutopic endometrial environments. These effects provide mechanistic links to persistent pain and infertility, although fibrosis is neither the sole determinant of symptoms nor a uniform feature across lesion phenotypes. This Mini Review integrates evidence from experimental models, human pathology, and single-cell studies; identifies uncertainties in cellular lineage, lesion chronology, and outcome attribution; and discusses therapeutic implications. Conventional hormonal and surgical treatment remains central, whereas antifibrotic, immunomodulatory, and complementary approaches require mechanism-based clinical validation. Progress will depend on standardized fibrosis phenotyping, longitudinal and spatial sampling, patient-derived multicellular models, and trials that align biological targets with pain, fertility, and recurrence outcomes.

Article.ArticleTitle: Biofilm state transitions: quorum sensing inhibition and network destabilization.

Abstract.AbstractText: Biofilms are traditionally viewed as surface-associated, extracellular polymeric substance (EPS)-encased aggregates. Here, we present a theoretical perspective positioning biofilm formation as a coordinated regulatory state transition, drawing on a synthesis of published transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolic studies that document systemic reprogramming of gene regulatory networks, second-messenger signaling (e.g., cyclic di-GMP), quorum sensing circuits, and metabolic flux distribution. Spatial stratification within biofilms generates metabolically distinct subpopulations-including persisters and dormant cells-that enhance collective robustness. Using Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium as a model organism, we formalize quorum sensing inhibition (QSI) as one plausible bifurcation control parameter, with its destabilizing effects described by a coarse-grained phenomenological model governed by cooperativity, population density, and signal decay rates. We show, through bifurcation analysis and cross-referencing with published experimental biofilm disruption studies, that sufficiently strong signal-decay-type QSI can collapse the high-signal biofilm attractor without imposing strong bactericidal pressure. This network-centric perspective elucidates how destabilization of collective regulatory circuits-rather than direct cell killing-can enhance therapeutic susceptibility. Additionally, the framework provides a conceptual basis for combinatorial strategies integrating antivirulence interventions with conventional antimicrobials, with the potential to reduce the pace of resistance evolution by targeting cooperative rather than essential traits. Predictions arising from this framework require direct experimental validation to establish quantitative accuracy. KEY POINTS: • Biofilms can be conceptualized as coordinated regulatory attractor states sustained by multilayered feedback coupling. • QSI is formalized as one plausible bifurcation control parameter capable of destabilizing the high-commitment biofilm state when implemented as signal-degradation-type inhibition. • Network destabilization may enhance antimicrobial susceptibility while imposing lower evolutionary pressure than direct bactericidal approaches.

Article.ArticleTitle: Emerging frontiers for AI in single-cell genomics.

Abstract.AbstractText: We are just over a decade into the single-cell revolution in biology, which has been coupled to the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in single-cell genomics. Most early single-cell RNA embedding models and subsequent "foundation models"-representational models pretrained on large single-cell datasets-did not gain wide traction among experimental biologists. However, as massive single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) atlas efforts ramp up, there is a clear rationale for exploiting AI models to interpret new datasets in the context of vast existing data resources. Meanwhile, the advent of single-cell epigenetic/multiomic assays and Perturb-seq technologies presents new opportunities for AI modeling. Here, we review AI embedding and foundation models for scRNA-seq and single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (scATAC-seq), extensive machine-learning efforts to exploit single-cell multiome in regulatory genomics, and AI strategies to learn "virtual cell" models from Perturb-seq, ending with a description of current limitations of single-cell AI models and an outlook for future advances.

Article.ArticleTitle: Programming brain endothelial identity: Transcription factor and genome engineering approaches to improve iPSC-derived BBB models.

Abstract.AbstractText: Human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived brain endothelial-like cells (iBECs) serve as important human relevant in vitro blood-brain barrier (BBB) models for evaluating central nervous system (CNS)-targeted therapies. However, conventional differentiation protocols often generate heterogeneous populations constrained by incomplete endothelial maturation. Overcoming these limitations requires precise control over developmental gene regulatory networks throughout differentiation. This review examines transcription factor-based forward reprogramming strategies designed to induce brain endothelial cell fate and prime BBB identity. Integrating these approaches with novel genome engineering tools enables the rational design of next generation BBB models with improved physiological fidelity and predictive power for CNS therapeutic discovery and validation.

Article.ArticleTitle: Web servers and bioinformatics tools for cancer research: A review.

Abstract.AbstractText: The rapid expansion of high-throughput technologies and multi-omics profiling has transformed cancer research by enabling systematic characterization of genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, immunological, and pharmacological features of tumors. These diverse molecular alterations contribute to tumor initiation, progression, heterogeneity, treatment response, and resistance, creating a need for computational resources capable of integrating and interpreting complex cancer datasets. Consequently, numerous bioinformatics resources have been developed to organize, analyze, and interpret cancer-related molecular and clinical data, encompassing expression profiling, survival analysis, regulatory network reconstruction, epigenetic annotation, immune analysis, and drug-response assessment. In this review, we systematically examine and comparatively evaluate cancer-focused bioinformatics resources according to their data coverage, analytical capabilities, evidence strength, limitations, and appropriate use cases. We further distinguish databases, analytical web servers, prediction tools, and integrated analysis platforms and discuss their respective applications and limitations. Overall, this review provides a practical framework for selecting and interpreting cancer bioinformatics resources while highlighting key challenges in data integration, evidence validation, reproducibility, and clinical translation.

Article.ArticleTitle: Reprogramming microglia via ShK-modified extracellular vesicles promotes immunomodulation and functional recovery after spinal cord injury.

Abstract.AbstractText: Microglia play a dual role in tissue repair and inflammatory responses following spinal cord injury (SCI), rendering the regulation of their immune activity a key therapeutic objective during disease progression. Single‑cell RNA sequencing revealed a significant upregulation of Kv1.3 expression in microglia following SCI, implicating this channel in the initiation of early neuroinflammation. To selectively target Kv1.3, engineered extracellular vesicles displaying ShK (ShK-EVs), a highly selective Kv1.3‑blocking peptide, were developed. These ShK‑EVs efficiently accumulated at the lesion site and were preferentially internalized by activated microglia. Integrated high‑throughput miRNA sequencing and proteomic profiling indicated that ShK‑EVs possess substantial neurorepair potential. Mechanistically, ShK‑EVs suppressed M1‑type microglial polarization and reduced the secretion of pro‑inflammatory cytokines by modulating the JAK/STAT signaling pathway. This modulation resulted in reduced tissue cavitation and neuronal apoptosis, enhanced neuronal survival and axonal regeneration, and ultimately led to a significant improvement in motor function in SCI mice. Taken together, these findings identify Kv1.3 as a key regulator of microglial activation after SCI and provide a novel, targeted therapeutic strategy using ShK‑EVs, offering new perspectives on immunomodulation of the injury microenvironment and functional neural recovery.

Article.ArticleTitle: Ion Channels in Cardiac Non-Excitable Cells: From Single-Cell Atlases to Disease.

Abstract.AbstractText: Cardiovascular disease is shaped not only by cardiomyocyte excitability but also by electrophysiological and membrane-signaling programs in cardiac fibroblasts, endothelial cells, mural cells, immune cells, and adipocytes. Recent single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomic, and disease-atlas studies have revealed broad expression of ion-channel transcripts across these non-excitable cardiac cell populations. However, transcript detection alone does not establish functional channel activity, cell-state specificity, or therapeutic relevance. This narrative Review therefore focuses on mechanistically supported channel-cell-disease axes rather than providing an exhaustive catalogue of ion channels detected in cardiac non-myocytes. We synthesize evidence for mechanosensitive channels, transient receptor potential channels, calcium-entry pathways, acid-sensing channels, and potassium, sodium, and chloride channels, as well as connexin hemichannels and pannexin channels. We emphasize studies in which omics-based channel nomination is supported by functional validation through electrophysiology, Ca2+ imaging, mechanostimulation, pharmacological intervention, or cell-selective genetic perturbation. Particular attention is given to mechanisms linking mechanical stress, Ca2+ entry, membrane potential, cell-volume regulation, ATP release, immune activation, vascular tone, fibrosis, and metabolic dysfunction. We also identify key evidence gaps where expression-based observations require direct functional testing in human tissues and disease-relevant cardiac models. By distinguishing atlas-level association from causal channel function, this Review provides a framework for prioritizing non-myocyte ion-channel mechanisms as therapeutic targets in cardiovascular diseases.

Article.ArticleTitle: MYC-SNHG7-miR-34a-5p Feedback Loop Orchestrates GSDMD-Dependent Pyroptosis in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.

Abstract.AbstractText: Pyroptosis is an immunogenic form of regulated cell death mediated by NLRP3 inflammasome activation, caspase-1, and gasdermin D. Unlike apoptosis, pyroptosis promotes anti-tumor immunity through IL-1β and IL-18 release, making it a promising therapeutic target in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Although the SNHG7/miR-34a/SIRT1 axis has been experimentally linked to NLRP3-dependent pyroptosis, whether it functions as a systems-level regulatory module coordinating the balance between drug resistance and multiple cell-fate outcomes remains unknown. To address this question, we developed a network medicine framework using a Boolean network model integrating drug resistance, senescence, apoptosis, and pyroptosis pathways in HCC. The model was constructed from experimentally validated molecular interactions and independently validated using gain- and loss-of-function perturbation studies that were not used during model construction, demonstrating strong agreement with experimental observations. Our analysis identified a previously unreported MYC-SNHG7-miR-34a double-negative feedback loop, establishing miR-34a as a central regulatory hub controlling cell-fate decisions. Perturbation analysis predicted that SNHG7 inhibition shifts cells from drug resistance toward pyroptosis, identifying restoration of miR-34a activity as a potential strategy to induce immunogenic cell death. These findings provide a systems-level framework for therapeutic targeting of the MYC-SNHG7-miR-34a axis in HCC.

Article.ArticleTitle: Deoxythymidylate Kinase (DTYMK)-Driven Pyrimidine Hypermetabolism Is Associated with a Folate-Dependent Macrophage Programme in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer.

Abstract.AbstractText: Immune checkpoint blockade benefits only a minority of patients with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), and the tumour-intrinsic programmes that establish its immunosuppressive microenvironment remain poorly defined. Pyrimidine metabolism supplies nucleotides and one-carbon units in malignant cells, but whether it shapes the immune microenvironment is unknown. Integrating single-cell, bulk breast cancer transcriptomics with Xenium spatial transcriptomics, DTYMK knockdown, tumour-conditioned-medium co-culture and folate rescue, we found that pyrimidine pathway activity was elevated in the malignant epithelium of TNBC, within which we identified Epi4, a high-potency subpopulation coupling pyrimidine and folate metabolism and predicted to export folate. Furthermore, this folate was predicted to be taken up by FOLR2+ tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs) and was associated with S-adenosylmethionine(SAM)-dependent methylation signatures and MAFB activity. Spatially, Epi4 and FOLR2+ TAMs co-localised at the tumour-stroma margin, a region of reduced T-cell density. DTYMK depletion reduced tumour fitness and attenuated folate-mediated macrophage reprogramming, which was largely restored by exogenous folate. Here, we therefore identify a DTYMK-folate-MAFB axis in which tumour metabolic rewiring is associated with epigenetic reprogramming of macrophages.

Article.ArticleTitle: Inflammatory Network Remodeling in AML Is Driven by Neutrophil-Centric Self-Amplifying Circuits.

Abstract.AbstractText: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) progression involves remodeling of the bone marrow inflammatory microenvironment, yet prior studies have focused on individual cytokines rather than coordinated network-level communication. This study aimed to systematically map inflammatory network reprogramming in AML and develop a network-derived prognostic tool. Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on bone marrow samples from three newly diagnosed AML patients and six healthy donors (47,525 cells); ligand-receptor communication was then analyzed using CellChat. Communication dominance shifted from T-cells to myeloid populations, with networks restructured into neutrophil-centric computationally predicted self-amplifying circuits, exemplified by CXCL8-CXCR2 and CCL3-CCR1 axes. Despite the limited sample size of the scRNA-seq cohort (3 AML patients and 6 healthy donors), which may limit the generalizability of the detailed cellular and network findings, the subsequent protein-level Luminex validation in a larger cohort of 46 patients and 26 healthy controls provides robust support for the key findings. An inflammatory risk score (IRS) was constructed using LASSO-penalized Cox regression and evaluated for prognostic performance and integration with the European LeukemiaNet 2022 (ELN2022) classification. Luminex profiling confirmed dysregulation of key mediators, including reduced CCL3, CCL4, CXCL8, and IL-1A together with elevated CXCL10 in AML, and revealed substantial de-modularization of the cytokine correlation network. The IRS, based on CXCL8, CCL2, and IL-1A, achieved a concordance index of 0.729 for overall survival and stratified the ELN2022 intermediate-risk category into distinct prognostic subgroups. Inflammatory network pattern analysis provides a complementary dimension to genetic risk stratification in AML. The IRS captures microenvironment-derived prognostic information not reflected by current classification systems, though prospective multicenter validation is essential before clinical application.

Article.ArticleTitle: Cell Tropism-Related Gene Signatures in MDD Identified by Transcriptomic Analysis and Rat Model Validation.

Abstract.AbstractText: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is associated with immune dysregulation, but the contribution of chemotaxis-related genes remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to identify chemotaxis-related signatures in MDD and evaluate their diagnostic relevance. Two peripheral-blood microarray datasets (GSE76826 and GSE38206) were integrated after batch correction, and differentially expressed genes were intersected with the GOBP_TAXIS gene set. Hub genes were selected using random forest and SVM-RFE and evaluated by logistic regression, ROC, calibration, and decision curve analyses. Immune-cell abundance, molecular subtypes, single-nucleus expression, and in silico gene-knockout effects were further examined, followed by qRT-PCR and Western blot validation in a CUMS rat model. The integrated cohort included 21 controls and 29 MDD cases. GOBP_TAXIS activity was increased in MDD (p < 0.001), and seven candidate genes yielded three upregulated hub genes (CXCL2, NRG1, and C3AR1). The fixed three-gene model yielded an exploratory AUC of 0.889 in the development cohort. All three genes correlated positively with monocytes/neutrophils and negatively with T cells. Single-cell analysis revealed cell-specific enrichment, while in silico knockout simulations predicted transcriptional changes involving RORB and NTNG1 following virtual perturbation of CXCL2 and NRG1. Animal experiments confirmed consistent upregulation at both transcriptional and translational levels. CXCL2, NRG1, and C3AR1 represent candidate chemotaxis-related biomarkers for MDD and are associated with distinct immune-cell abundance patterns and inflammatory signatures, warranting further functional validation.

Article.ArticleTitle: Development and validation of a ferroptosis and metabolic reprogramming gene signature for risk stratification in bladder urothelial carcinoma: A retrospective multicohort study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Bladder urothelial carcinoma (BLCA) is clinically and molecularly heterogeneous, and conventional clinicopathologic factors do not fully reflect the biological variation associated with survival. We aimed to develop and externally evaluate a prognostic signature based on genes related to both ferroptosis and metabolic reprogramming and to examine its clinical and biological associations. The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)-BLCA transcriptomic and clinical data were used for candidate-gene identification and model development. A 10-gene least absolute shrinkage and selection operator Cox signature was evaluated by complete-pipeline bootstrap validation. After platform harmonization, the same coefficients and TCGA-derived cutoff were applied to GSE13507 and GSE48075. Clinical adjustment, stage-specific analyses, immune analyses accounting for the IFNG score contribution, tumor purity, and molecular subtype, exploratory drug-response prediction, and expression analysis in 15 paired institutional tumor and adjacent tissues were performed. The signature comprised JUN, IFNG, CAV1, SREBF1, G6PD, TFRC, SCD, ZEB1, SLC7A11, and WWTR1. In TCGA-BLCA (401 patients; 176 deaths), the high-risk group had poorer overall survival (hazard ratio [HR] = 2.313; 95% confidence interval = 1.697-3.154; P < .001). The fixed TCGA cutoff also identified high-risk groups in GSE13507 (165 patients; 69 deaths; HR = 2.202; P = .0010) and GSE48075 (73 patients; 45 deaths; HR = 2.476; P = .0082). The 10-gene RiskScore yielded 1-, 3-, and 5-year areas under the curve of 0.644, 0.657, and 0.668 in TCGA-BLCA; the corresponding values ranged from 0.583 to 0.696 in the external cohorts. RiskScore remained associated with survival after adjustment for age, sex, and stage in TCGA (HR per standard-deviation increase, 1.573; P < .001). In the paired institutional cohort, 5 genes differed between tumor and adjacent tissues at a false discovery rate below 0.05, and 9 of 10 genes showed expression directions concordant with TCGA. Enrichment analyses highlighted oxidative-stress and metabolic pathways; several immune and checkpoint associations remained after sensitivity analyses, and exploratory modeling identified risk-group differences in predicted drug sensitivity. The 10-gene signature consistently stratified overall survival across TCGA-BLCA and 2 independent Gene Expression Omnibus cohorts. Its associations with clinical outcome, paired-tissue expression, and immune features support further investigation of ferroptosis-related metabolic heterogeneity in BLCA.

Journal.Title: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology

Article.ArticleTitle: Dynamic increases in p53 expression suppress human myoblast differentiation.

Abstract.AbstractText: Skeletal muscle maintenance and regeneration are highly regulated by cell fate decisions made by muscle stem cells and their progeny, myoblasts. Although the transcription factor p53 is well known for its role in cellular stress responses, cell cycle regulation, and tumor prevention, emerging evidence suggests that p53 also plays a critical role in determining whether myoblasts differentiate into muscle fibers or remain single cells that re-enter quiescence to replenish the satellite cell pool. Most previous studies, however, have relied on static, population-level measurements of p53, leaving its dynamic real-time behavior in individual myoblasts largely unexplored. In this study, we use single cell time-lapse microscopy to investigate temporal patterns of p53 activity in fluorescently-tagged immortalized human myoblasts induced to differentiate. We find that cells in which p53 levels increase more quickly and accumulate to higher amplitudes tend to remain single cells rather than differentiate and fuse into myofibers. Understanding how p53 dynamics influence muscle cell fate may provide fundamental insights into muscle maintenance, regeneration, and degenerative disease.

Article.ArticleTitle: DEG2MOL: Conditional Latent Flow Matching for Transcriptome-Guided de novo Drug Design.

Abstract.AbstractText: Transcriptomic profiles capture cellular responses to perturbations, offering a principled foundation for biologically grounded de novo drug design. However, existing transcriptome-guided generative approaches remain limited in biological specificity, transcriptomic coverage, and evaluation across diverse perturbation contexts. Here, we propose DEG2MOL, a biologically grounded conditioning framework that encodes differentially expressed gene profiles through a Gene Ontology (GO)-informed encoder and maps this representation into the latent space of a frozen, pre-trained scaffold-aware VAE via conditional latent flow matching. When benchmarked against five baseline models, DEG2MOL ranked first by rank-sum aggregation of six metrics in both the random- and scaffold-split evaluations. For two representative compound conditions, GO-informed encoder activations were accompanied by enrichment of the corresponding target-engaging pharmacophores among the generated molecules. In docking case studies of two compound-target pairs, generated molecules showed favorable predicted docking scores and reference-associated contacts. DEG2MOL also generated molecules from shRNA knockdown, CRISPR knockout, and Perturb-seq profiles without additional training, indicating transfer across the perturbation types and profiling platforms evaluated. At the transcriptional level, an in silico gene-expression analysis showed that the predicted signatures of generated molecules were more similar to those of target-matched inhibitors than to those of unrelated inhibitors. The data and code are available at https://github.com/KU-MedAI/DEG2MOL.

Article.ArticleTitle: Transcription factor-driven metabolic stratification reveals glycolytic and lipogenic subtypes with distinct prognostic and functional features in pancreatic cancer.

Abstract.AbstractText: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) exhibits profound molecular and metabolic heterogeneity associated with distinct phenotypic states. However, the contribution of transcription factor (TF)-driven regulatory programs to metabolic subtype stratification remains poorly understood. This study aims to determine whether TF-based classification can identify prognostically relevant glycolytic and lipogenic PDAC subtypes.

Bulk transcriptomic data from multiple PDAC cohorts and single-cell RNA sequencing data were integrated to characterize TF-associated metabolic heterogeneity. Metabolic signatures and TFs were quantified using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) and AddModule Score (AMS). Differential expression, enrichment analysis, integrative bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analysis, and deep neural network-based metabolic flux modeling were performed to investigate metabolic programs and functional differences between TF-defined subtypes. Additionally, RNA interference, RT-qPCR, lipid droplets staining, lactate assay, and transwell assays were used to evaluate the roles of TP63 in metabolic regulation.

Glycolytic and lipogenic TF-defined metabolic subtypes were identified across multiple independent PDAC cohorts. These subtypes exhibited distinct metabolic programs, differentiation states, and prognostic outcomes. The glycolytic TF-defined subtype was associated with worse prognosis and differentiation, whereas the lipogenic TF-defined subtype exhibited more favorable clinical features. Integration of public bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses, together with deep neural network-based metabolic flux modeling, revealed consistent metabolic heterogeneity at both cellular and functional levels. Notably, TP63 was identified as a potential regulator of glycolytic-lipogenic metabolic reprogramming in PDAC.

TF-based classification delineates glycolytic and lipogenic subtypes in PDAC, underscoring the critical role of TF-regulated metabolic programs in patient stratification. These findings highlight the prognostic significance of glycolytic and lipogenic metabolic heterogeneity and support the development of metabolism-targeted therapeutic strategies.

Article.ArticleTitle: Progress of metabolomics-centric multi-omics research in medicine.

Abstract.AbstractText: Metabolomics reveals molecular changes at the metabolic level during biological processes. Recent advancements, particularly through integration with other omics and artificial intelligence (AI), are advancing metabolic data analysis and multi-omics interpretation. This review introduces a "metabolomics-centric" paradigm as a conceptual framework for multi-omics integration, positioning metabolic readouts as the functional anchor for interpreting genotype-phenotype relationships. It also chronicles the evolution and medical applications of integration technologies. Our discussion first traces the field's evolution from bulk to single-cell and spatial methodologies, next surveys integration strategies to uncover mechanistic insights, and finally examines how AI-driven multimodal data integration and AI-optimized metabolomics workflows tackle persistent biological and computational challenges. Looking forward, this review identifies the AI virtual cell as a pivotal future direction for metabolomics-based multi-omics integration, calling for increased attention to its development to simulate dynamic molecular phenotypic networks within a multi-omics context.

Journal.Title: Extracellular vesicles and circulating nucleic acids

Article.ArticleTitle: Artificial intelligence for extracellular vesicle engineering and therapeutic design.

Abstract.AbstractText: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are promising platforms for next-generation drug delivery and regenerative therapeutics, yet biological heterogeneity, limited targeting specificity, variable cargo composition, and continued reliance on empirical optimization hinder clinical translation. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers new opportunities to make EV engineering more predictive and data-driven. Building on prior work in AI-assisted EV delivery and emerging virtual-EV modeling, this review presents an evidence-aware, multiscale framework that integrates parental-cell programming, vesicle design, recipient-system modeling, and experimental feedback. At the source level, AI virtual cells (AIVCs) may help predict how perturbations to parental cells influence EV biogenesis and composition. At the vesicle level, AI-guided approaches may support cargo prioritization, surface engineering, and loading optimization. At the recipient level, digital twin models could help simulate EV uptake, intracellular trafficking, microenvironmental interactions, and downstream therapeutic responses. These components may ultimately be integrated with experimental validation into iterative design-test-refinement workflows. Importantly, this review distinguishes direct EV-specific evidence from technologies transferable from adjacent fields and concepts that remain prospective. By defining these evidence boundaries and linking them to key challenges in data quality, model interpretability, manufacturing, and validation, this framework provides a practical roadmap for advancing AI-enabled EV therapeutics from conceptual modeling to testable, translationally relevant engineering strategies.

Article.ArticleTitle: A Metabolic Cluster-Derived Risk Model for Prognostic Stratification, Immunometabolic Profiling, and Therapeutic Sensitivity Prediction in Prostate Cancer.

Abstract.AbstractText: Metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of prostate cancer; however, the clinical utility of metabolism-related genes for prognostic stratification remains limited.

Prostate cancer patients from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) databases were stratified into metabolism-associated clusters based on metabolism-related gene expression. Genes differentially expressed between clusters were used to construct a prognostic risk model via least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. Associations with clinicopathological features, genomic alterations, metabolic activity, immune status, and therapeutic response were systematically evaluated. Computational analyses included tumor immune dysfunction and exclusion (TIDE) and the immunophenoscore for predicting immunotherapy response, pRRophetic and CellMiner for assessing drug sensitivity, and the Connectivity Map for screening candidate compounds. Exploratory assessments were performed using immunohistochemistry (IHC) in a 20-patient cohort with follow-up data and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) in an independent 14-patient cohort.

Two metabolism-associated clusters with distinct survival outcomes and molecular features were identified. A three-gene signature stratified patients into high- and low-risk groups, with the high-risk group showing poorer survival, greater tumor aggressiveness, elevated tumor mutational burden and microsatellite instability, and enhanced metabolic pathway activity. This group also exhibited an immunosuppressive microenvironment and was predicted to have reduced responsiveness to some immunotherapies and endocrine therapies, along with increased resistance to specific chemotherapeutic agents. In silico analyses suggested several candidate small molecules for further evaluation in the high-risk group. The IHC- and qPCR-based exploratory experiments showed associations between the derived scores and clinicopathological features, providing preliminary support for the transcriptomic signature.

This metabolic cluster-derived three-gene model may support prognostic stratification and characterization of immunometabolic heterogeneity in prostate cancer. The observed associations between metabolic heterogeneity and computationally predicted therapeutic sensitivity provide a rationale for further investigation of potential treatment strategies.

OtherAbstract.AbstractText: People with prostate cancer can have very different outcomes despite similar medical profiles. Differences in how cancer cells use nutrients and produce energy—their metabolism—may help explain this variation. Researchers want to understand how these differences relate to the risk of poor outcomes. In this study, researchers analyzed gene expression data from 776 people with prostate cancer and classified them into two distinct metabolic subgroups. They then developed a model based on three genes. The high-risk group showed higher activity in metabolism-related pathways, features consistent with reduced antitumor immune activity, and molecular characteristics associated with poorer treatment response. Computational analyses also suggested candidate small-molecule compounds for further study, and the researchers evaluated the model using tumor samples from two separate groups of 20 and 14 patients. This approach links metabolic differences with clinical outcomes, immune characteristics, and treatment-related features and may help assess risk and offer ideas to test in future clinical studies.

Article.ArticleTitle: Targeting the MAT2A-SAM axis increases platinum sensitivity in ovarian cancer by impairing DNA repair and stemness.

Abstract.AbstractText: Metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming drives platinum resistance and recurrence in high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSC), presenting a critical clinical challenge. Acquired platinum resistance has been linked to altered DNA methylation, a process requiring S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), synthesized by methionine adenosyltransferase 2A (MAT2A) from methionine metabolism. However, how the MAT2A-SAM axis coordinates metabolic-epigenetic remodeling in HGSC remains unclear. We demonstrate that MAT2A-driven SAM synthesis is essential for platinum-induced DNA methylation dynamics and ovarian cancer stem cells (OCSCs) enrichment. High MAT2A expression correlates with poor progression-free survival in HGSC patients, while genetic knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of MAT2A increases cisplatin sensitivity in HGSC cells. Genome-wide DNA methylation profiling showed that cisplatin reshaped the methylome with prominent hypermethylation at promoter regions, which was reversed by MAT2A knockdown. Transcription factors predicted from differential methylation were enriched in platinum resistance, DNA repair, and stemness pathways. Mechanistically, disrupting MAT2A-SAM axis suppresses a novel SAMTOR-mTOR-S6K-FANCD2 signaling pathway. This blockade leads to the accumulation of R-loops, attenuates both homologous recombination (HR) and non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) repair pathways, and enhanced platinum-induced cell death. Furthermore, transcriptomic analysis of paired primary and recurrent HGSC tumors links MAT2A increase to elevated OCSC features during recurrence. Consistently, MAT2A inhibition prevents cisplatin-increased OCSC population and sphere-forming capacity in vitro, both of which are rescued by exogenous SAM supplementation. Together, our findings identify the MAT2A-SAM axis as a pivotal metabolic-epigenetic regulator of the DNA damage response and cancer stemness, establishing MAT2A inhibition as a therapeutic strategy to enhance platinum sensitivity in HGSC.

Cisplatin remodels the HGSC cell methylome with predominant promoter hypermethylationMAT2A-SAM is essential for platinum-induced methylome remodeling and OCSC enrichmentMAT2A loss impairs activation of HR and NHEJ repair via mTOR-S6K-FANCD2 signalingMAT2A inhibition increases platinum sensitivity in both MTAP-proficient and -deficient HGSC cells tested.

Article.ArticleTitle: Differential evolution of neuroinflammatory remodeling programs related to scar formation and regeneration in spinal cord injury: A cross-species multi-omics analysis.

Abstract.AbstractText: Spinal cord injury in mammals often transitions from an acute inflammatory response to persistent neuroinflammatory and scar-associated remodeling, whereas zebrafish attenuate injury-induced inflammatory programs during regenerative repair. The molecular programs underlying these divergent outcomes remain incompletely understood. In this study, we integrated phase-aligned mouse and zebrafish spinal cord injury datasets using single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomics, spatial transcriptomics, pathway and regulon analyses, expression-based ligand-receptor co-expression analysis, machine-learning validation, chromatin-accessibility profiling, in silico perturbation modeling, and mouse tissue validation. Cross-species analysis revealed a conserved injury-responsive program associated with secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1) and CD44, but with distinct temporal trajectories between species. In mouse spinal cord injury, Spp1 and Cd44 expression remained elevated from acute injury through scar-associated stages and was enriched within lesion-associated myeloid and glial-immune microenvironments. Persistent SPP1-CD44-associated expression was accompanied by inflammatory signaling, reactive gliosis, fibrotic remodeling, and sustained immune-niche remodeling. In zebrafish, spp1 and cd44a were similarly induced during the early injury response but declined during regenerative recovery, consistent with attenuation and reorganization of inflammatory programs rather than absence of early injury activation. Machine-learning analyses supported the cross-dataset reproducibility of SPP1-CD44-related injury-state features across two mouse spinal cord injury datasets. Regulon, perturbation-associated, and chromatin-accessibility analyses further positioned Spp1 within an injury-responsive regulatory context associated with signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 and SMARCA4 (SWI/SNF related, matrix associated, actin dependent regulator of chromatin, subfamily a, member 4) states and identified perturbation-sensitive accessibility changes at the Spp1 promoter. Mouse spinal cord injury tissue validation confirmed increased SPP1 and CD44 protein expression after injury and localized enhanced SPP1 signal to ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1-positive lesion-associated myeloid regions. Together, these findings suggest that mammalian spinal cord injury scarring is associated with persistence of a conserved SPP1-CD44-associated neuroinflammatory remodeling program, whereas attenuation of the corresponding program accompanies regenerative spinal cord repair in zebrafish. This cross-species framework provides molecular insights and candidate regulatory programs for future studies aimed at promoting inflammatory resolution and neural repair after spinal cord injury.

Article.ArticleTitle: Virtual cells: progress and challenges from mechanistic modeling to data-driven integration.

Abstract.AbstractText: Virtual cells aim to represent cellular states computationally and predict responses to genetic, chemical, environmental, temporal, and spatial conditions. For comparative purposes, this review uses state encoding (E), state transition (T), and observation decoding (D) as a conceptual abstraction spanning explicit mechanistic models, data-driven foundation and perturbation models, multimodal systems, and spatial and multiscale simulation. We examine model boundaries, data foundations, resource disclosure, out-of-distribution evaluation, causal evidence, and experimental validation. Independent benchmarks show that parameter count and training-set size do not automatically yield robust out-of-distribution generalization, while transcriptomic representations alone do not capture the full functional state of a cell. Trustworthy virtual cells will require perturbation-responsive transitions, cross-modal alignment, continuous-time dynamics, mechanistic constraints, calibrated uncertainty, independent experimental validation, and, where appropriate, closed-loop experimental feedback.

Article.ArticleTitle: Cell-resolved genetic risk reveals hyperandrogenism-associated immune and metabolic rewiring in the PMOS follicular microenvironment.

Abstract.AbstractText: Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) is a leading cause of anovulatory infertility. Although follicular developmental arrest is a defining feature of PMOS, the cell-type-specific mechanisms linking genetic susceptibility, endocrine imbalance and follicular microenvironmental dysfunction remain incompletely understood, particularly across clinical subtypes.

We performed single-cell RNA sequencing of preovulatory follicular-fluid cells from healthy controls and women with uncomplicated PMOS, hyperandrogenic PMOS and metformin-treated insulin-resistant PMOS. We integrated these data with GWAS-derived disease relevance scores and ovarian chromatin-accessibility annotations to map genetic risk to follicular cell populations and regulatory programmes. Ligand-receptor analyses were used to infer intercellular communication networks. Transcriptomic metabolic findings were further assessed by follicular-fluid metabolic and steroid-hormone measurements, DHT-treated granulosa-cell functional assays, and reanalysis of a DHEA-induced mouse PMOS-like ovarian dataset.

We generated a single-cell atlas of the PMOS follicular microenvironment comprising 220,983 high-quality cells. Granulosa cells showed the strongest enrichment of PMOS-related genetic risk, with regulatory-genetic support from ovarian snATAC-seq integration. Among granulosa cell states, a GC2_CYP19A1⁺ population was preferentially associated with hyperandrogenic PMOS and displayed a transcriptional programme characterized by steroidogenic remodelling coupled to reduced energy-metabolic activity. Biochemical profiling supported this endocrine-metabolic imbalance, showing increased follicular-fluid androstenedione (ASD) and estrone, reduced estradiol and E2/ASD ratio, decreased ATP, citrate and fumarate hydratase activity, and increased lactate and β-hydroxybutyrate. Prolonged DHT exposure impaired granulosa-cell mitochondrial respiration, ATP production and mitochondrial membrane potential. In parallel, PMOS subtypes showed immune remodelling and altered ligand-receptor signalling, with hyperandrogenic PMOS associated with increased inflammatory signalling and reduced homeostatic or tissue-repair pathways. Reanalysis of a DHEA-induced mouse ovarian dataset provided supportive evidence for androgen-associated steroidogenic pathway perturbation.

This study provides a cell-resolved framework linking PMOS genetic susceptibility to endocrine-metabolic and immune remodelling in the preovulatory follicular microenvironment. The identification of a hyperandrogen-associated GC2_CYP19A1⁺ state highlights a candidate cellular programme in which steroidogenic imbalance is coupled to impaired granulosa-cell bioenergetics. These findings provide a resource for future validation and may inform microenvironment-guided stratification of PMOS and the development of strategies aimed at restoring follicular function.

Article.ArticleTitle: Aging, regeneration, and peripheral nerve repair: Integrated multi-omics biomarkers and AI-enabled therapeutic discovery approaches.

Abstract.AbstractText: Peripheral nerve injury (PNI) remains a major cause of long-term sensory and motor dysfunction, imposing a substantial clinical and socioeconomic burden worldwide. Although peripheral nerves possess intrinsic regenerative capacity, functional recovery is often incomplete because of the complex interplay among axonal degeneration, Schwann cell plasticity, neuroimmune responses, extracellular matrix remodeling, metabolic reprogramming, remyelination, and target reinnervation. Recent advances in transcriptomics, proteomics, epigenomics, metabolomics, and single-cell technologies have expanded molecular characterization of nerve degeneration and regeneration, revealing numerous candidate biomarkers and therapeutic targets. However, biological heterogeneity, fragmented datasets, and the lack of robust predictive frameworks still limit translation into clinical practice. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the cellular and molecular mechanisms governing peripheral nerve repair and examine emerging biomarker classes associated with regenerative competence, neuroinflammation, remyelination, and functional recovery. We also discuss therapeutic strategies targeting Schwann cell reprogramming, axonal growth, immune modulation, metabolic adaptation, and remodeling of the regenerative microenvironment. We further examine how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) may support multi-omics integration, biomarker prioritization, outcome prediction, and therapeutic target discovery, while emphasizing that PNI-specific clinical validation remains limited. We propose a systems-level framework that links molecular signatures with clinical outcomes and highlights the potential of AI-enabled multimodal analytics to support translational research. Age-related molecular variation should be incorporated as an additional analytical dimension, allowing comparison of regenerative and non-regenerative signatures across younger and older tissues. Together, these approaches provide a framework for testing age-aware molecular markers and computational models in future translational studies.

Article.ArticleTitle: Cytokine context shapes antigen-presenting and matrix-producing states of cancer-associated fibroblasts.

Abstract.AbstractText: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) exhibit remarkable functional heterogeneity, with conserved subtypes observed across diverse malignancies. However, their shared roles in shaping the tumor microenvironment (TME) and their dynamic plasticity remain incompletely understood. In this study, through integrated single-cell and spatial transcriptomic profiling across four cancer types, we identified two distinct immunomodulatory CAF states, termed antigen-presenting CAFs (apCAFs) and matrix-producing CAFs (mCAFs). Across multiple solid tumors, apCAFs were associated with enhanced anti-tumor immune features and favorable prognosis, whereas mCAFs were associated with immunosuppressive characteristics and poorer clinical outcomes. Spatial analyses revealed distinct localization patterns of apCAFs and mCAFs within the TME. Functionally, patient-derived apCAFs promoted T-cell migration, proliferation, and activation, whereas mCAFs suppressed these responses in vitro. Pan-cancer analyses further revealed a strong inverse correlation between apCAF and mCAF abundance across tumor tissues. Mechanistically, IFN-γ and TGF-β-associated signaling contexts were linked to distinct CAF transcriptional programs, with IFN-γ promoting apCAF-associated features and TGF-β favoring mCAF-associated features, suggesting a potential role of cytokine context in shaping CAF state heterogeneity. Clinically, apCAFs correlated with favorable immunotherapy response, whereas mCAFs predicted poor therapeutic outcomes. Collectively, these findings identify conserved immunomodulatory CAF subtypes across cancers, reveal distinct cytokine-associated CAF programs, and support stromal reprogramming as a promising strategy to enhance immunotherapy efficacy.

Article.ArticleTitle: Absence of a prolonged macrophage and B cell response inhibits heart regeneration in the Mexican cavefish.

Abstract.AbstractText: A balanced immune response after cardiac injury is crucial to successful heart regeneration, but knowledge of what distinguishes a regenerative from a scarring response is still limited. The Mexican cavefish Astyanax mexicanus provides a unique comparative model to study heart regeneration and scarring within a single species. Astyanax surface-dwelling fish are capable of heart regeneration, whereas, like the human heart, their cave-dwelling Pachón counterparts form a permanent scar. Using single-cell transcriptomics and immune perturbations, we identify two distinct and largely sequential immune mechanisms driving regeneration in surface fish. First, late-present macrophages are actively phagocytic, and pharmacological inhibition of phagocytosis disrupts scar clearance and regeneration. Second, B cells recruited from 7 days post-injury promote cardiomyocyte cell progression into mitosis, and their inhibition with Acalabrutinib significantly impairs cardiomyocyte proliferation and regeneration. This B cell-dependent mechanism is conserved in zebrafish. Our findings reveal two independent late immune mechanisms distinguishing regenerative from non-regenerative cardiac repair, offering insights for potential therapeutic strategies to enhance heart regeneration in mammals.

Article.ArticleTitle: Single-cell eQTL Mendelian randomization reveals the monocyte-associated PRKCB-CTSL axis as a candidate regulatory pathway and potential therapeutic target in rheumatoid arthritis.

Abstract.AbstractText: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) involves persistent immune dysregulation, but cell-specific genetically regulated pathways remain unclear. We integrated cell-specific genetic and multi-omics evidence to prioritize candidate regulatory pathways.

cis-eQTLs from 17 immune-cell populations were integrated with RA GWAS data by two-sample Mendelian randomization. Transcriptomics, WGCNA, and machine-learning feature selection identified convergent candidates. Single-cell and virtual perturbation analyses assessed cellular localization and downstream changes. Molecular docking and dynamics computationally prioritized compounds, and knockdown/rescue experiments evaluated the PRKCB-CTSL relationship.

Eleven candidates had convergent genetic and transcriptomic support. PRKCB was retained by LASSO, SVM, and random forest and preferentially expressed in monocytes. Virtual perturbation implicated CTSL and antigen-processing/presentation pathways. PRKCB knockdown reduced CTSL expression and NF-κB phosphorylation, whereas CTSL restoration partially rescued NF-κB phosphorylation. Separately, structure-based analyses computationally prioritized ursodiol for the most favorable predicted PRKCB interaction among evaluated compounds.

Genetic, transcriptomic, single-cell, computational, and in vitro evidence supports monocyte-associated PRKCB-CTSL as a candidate regulatory pathway in RA. Further mechanistic and in vivo studies are required to establish its causal and pharmacological relevance. Key Points • Multi-omics analysis identified 11 key RA-associated targets. • RA was classified into two molecular subtypes with distinct immune features. • PRKCB was identified as the core target enriched in monocytes. • The PRKCB-CTSL axis may drive RA inflammation, and ursodiol showed therapeutic potential.

Article.ArticleTitle: Patient-derived organoids for precision oncology in colorectal cancer: from tumor modeling to clinical translation.

Abstract.AbstractText: Precision oncology in colorectal cancer (CRC) has been profoundly informed by genomic and transcriptomic profiling, yet molecular stratification remains only partially predictive of therapeutic benefit. This reflects a broader challenge: moving from static molecular information to dynamic, adaptive, and time-resolved predictions of drug response for individual patients along their clinical history. In CRC, this challenge is compounded by extensive inter- and intratumoral heterogeneity, clonal evolution, chromosomal instability, phenotypic plasticity and tumor-microenvironment (TME) interactions, all of which reshape therapeutic vulnerabilities over time.Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) have emerged as a functional platform to address this gap, with CRC providing one of the most fertile contexts for their development and application. By preserving key histopathological, molecular, and phenotypic features of parental tumors while remaining experimentally tractable, expandable, and amenable to pharmacological and genetic perturbation, PDOs add a functional layer to precision oncology in CRC. Living organoid biobanks and ex vivo screening studies have shown that PDOs can capture interpatient heterogeneity, uncover mechanisms of sensitivity and resistance, and, in selected contexts, mirror clinical responses to chemotherapy and targeted agents. The same experimental tractability has made these systems powerful tools for investigating tumor initiation and clonal evolution, while enabling exploration of cellular plasticity through the lens of dynamic cellular hierarchies. In parallel, next-generation CRC organoid systems incorporating stromal and immune components may extend functional testing to TME-dependent processes, including response to immunotherapy.In this review, we discuss the conceptual foundations of organoid technology and its emergence as a functional precision oncology platform in CRC. We examine how CRC organoids have advanced understanding of tumor initiation, evolution, chromosomal instability, and phenotypic plasticity; summarize their applications in drug discovery, therapy-response prediction, and resistance modeling; and highlight the development of next-generation multicellular organoid systems incorporating immune and stromal components. Finally, we address the major technical, biological, and clinical challenges that must be overcome to translate PDO-based approaches into robust and clinically actionable tools for precision medicine.
